question: Death Valley's Racetrack Playa. Rocks, some heavier than a person, leave long trails across the dry lakebed. What moves them?
answer: Ice and a light breeze. A shallow winter pond freezes into a skin a few millimetres thick; when the morning sun breaks it into panels, a breeze pushes them and they shove the rocks along. GPS on the rocks caught it in 2013. The force was ordinary; the conditions were rare.
move: When nobody sees something happen, suspect rare conditions before huge forces.
ask: What do I explain with something dramatic when an ordinary cause on an unusual day would do?

clues.text: Trails run hundreds of metres. For decades nobody sees a rock move.
No footprints or tyre marks beside any trail, in mud that keeps every print.
New trails appear only in winter, after rain leaves a shallow pond.
2013, GPS on the rocks: they creep while the wind is a light breeze.
That morning, ice a few millimetres thick breaks into floating panels.

scene.why: No gale was blowing: the rocks moved in a breeze. Something else had to do the shoving.

reference: Norris et al., Sliding rocks on Racetrack Playa, Death Valley National Park: first observation of rocks in motion, PLOS ONE 9(8):e105948, 2014, doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0105948
